prompt: Match each situation to its fitting model

pairNotes.r: Spiral exists to buy down risk per cycle — that is its whole point.
pairNotes.u: A prototype answers one question fast; it is not a first draft of the product.

explanation: Stable → waterfall's cheap sequence; risky → spiral's risk cycles; doubtful → prototype the question before committing.

prompt: Order the waterfall phases
explanation: The lecture's phase order. Iterative waterfall keeps the order but adds feedback loops — a test failure can send work back to design.

prompt: Complete the WBS rule
instructions: Drag each word into its blank — or tap a word, then tap a blank.
text: A ___ breaks a project into ___ with ___ and ___ .
explanation: A WBS decomposes work into tasks, annotated with dependencies and milestones. Gantt charts and poker come later — they consume the WBS, they are not part of it.
hints: The acronym names the whole structure.

prompt: Put the planning workflow in order
instructions: Drag rows into sequence — one continuous drag does it. Alt+↑/↓ works from the keyboard.

items.label: Break the project into WBS tasks
Record dependencies in a task table
Compute ES/EF, LS/LF, slack, critical path

explanation: Decompose → estimate → order → draw → time-analyse. Every later step eats the earlier step's output, which is why a sloppy WBS poisons the whole plan.

prompt: In which diagram do the arrows represent activities?

distractor.0: In AON, activities are the nodes (boxes); arrows are only dependencies.
distractor.2: They encode the same project differently — work lives on nodes in one, arrows in the other.
distractor.3: Arrows mean 'must complete before', not data flow.

explanation: AOA puts work on arrows (nodes are instants, sometimes needing dummy tasks); AON puts work on nodes.

prompt: Complete the slack rule
text: Slack = ___ − ___ . The ___ path is the zero-slack chain.
explanation: Slack = LS − ES (equivalently LF − EF). The zero-slack chain is the critical path — the longest path, which sets the shortest possible duration.

prompt: Order the timing analysis
explanation: Forwards for earliest and duration, backwards for latest, subtract for slack, chain the zeros — then verify the chain sums to the duration.

prompt: Click the 10-week activity on the critical chain
instructions: Select the D task in the Project A network.
explanation: D (10 weeks) sits on A → D → F → G → H. It has zero slack: any slip delays the 25-week deadline.

prompt: Project duration equals the sum of all task durations.

distractor.0: Only the critical path's tasks sum to the duration — off-path work overlaps in time. 2022 Project A totals far more than 25 weeks of tasks.

explanation: False. Duration is the longest path through the network, not the sum of everything.

prompt: Order a sprint's events
explanation: Commit, steer, inspect the product with stakeholders, then improve the process. Review looks outward; retrospective looks inward.

prompt: Which event inspects the product with stakeholders?

distractor.0: Planning commits to the goal — inspection happens at the end.
distractor.1: Dailies steer the Developers' own plan.
distractor.3: The retrospective inspects the process, within the team only.

explanation: The review demos the increment to stakeholders and adapts the backlog; the retrospective follows and improves how the team works.

prompt: Scenario: a 'Done' card turns out defective
instructions: You are on a team with a WIP limit of 3. 'Search Courses' is Done — but a user reports it crashes on empty queries. Decide what happens next.

alert.text: Bug report lands: 'Search Courses' (in Done) crashes on empty queries. Review is full (3/3), Coding has 1 card. What do you do first?

options.label: Pull fresh work into Coding anyway
options.note: Starting new work while a defect escapes violates finish-before-start.

options.label: Move the card back to Coding/Testing and fix it within WIP
options.note: Done means accepted — a defective card re-enters the flow.

options.label: Ask to raise the WIP limit so everything fits
options.note: Raising WIP hides the constraint instead of resolving it.

rushed.text: Two streams now compete: the defect and the new feature. Review stays clogged; the crash reaches more users.
rushed.title: Split focus
rushed.debrief: WIP limits exist to force finishing over starting. New work while a known defect escapes multiplies rework.

limit.text: The board absorbs everything — columns swell to 5, 6, 7 cards. Nothing finishes; the pile-up signal is gone.
limit.title: Limit inflated
limit.debrief: A WIP limit you raise whenever it binds is decoration. The pile-up was the diagnosis; the fix was rebalancing toward Review.

fixing.text: The card is back in Coding/Testing and the crash is fixed. Review still holds 3 cards. How does the fix reach Done?

options.label: Merge it straight to Done — it was Done before
options.note: Fixes re-break things; the lecture says regressions re-occur.

options.label: Let it flow through Review and Awaiting Merge again

sloppy.text: The fix ships unreviewed and breaks saved searches. Another card travels backwards — the team now distrusts Done.
sloppy.title: Unreviewed merge
sloppy.debrief: Regression discipline is the point of the Review column. Every fix gets re-reviewed, or Done stops meaning accepted.

solid.text: Re-reviewed, re-merged, re-accepted. The board kept flowing because the team finished the defect before starting anything new.
solid.title: Discipline held
solid.debrief: Move Done defects back, respect WIP, re-review fixes. That is the whole Kanban contract in one incident.

explanation: Kanban incidents test one habit: finish before you start. The board's columns and WIP limit tell you exactly where defective work belongs.

prompt: Sort each sentence: function or characteristic?

left.label: 'Render them within 2 s on the lab PC'

explanation: Inputs-to-outputs versus a measurable bound on that function. The worksheet's two-question test decides every case.

prompt: Rebuild the story formula
text: As a ___ , I want ___ so that ___ .
explanation: Role, want, benefit — one sentence, all three present. 'The system' is never a role; 'clean code' is a task, not a user benefit.
hints: Who benefits — a real user, not the software.

prompt: 'As a database, I want indexes so that queries run fast' is a valid user story.

distractor.0: Stories are about users — people who use the software. A database is an implementation detail.

explanation: False. User-story common sense: stories serve real users. System internals belong in tasks, not stories.

prompt: Trigger or precondition?
text: The ___ starts the flow; the ___ must already be true.
explanation: Selecting 'plot data' triggers; being logged in pre-exists. Swapping them is the classic half-mark loss (2022 Q2.2a).

prompt: Reconstruct the happy-days flow
instructions: Plot-data scenario, five steps. Alternate actor and system.

items.label: System lists datasets for the credentials
User picks dataset, columns and chart style
System generates, displays and saves the PNG

explanation: Trigger → system lists → actor specifies → system produces → confirm. Every deviation branches to an extension, never into the main flow.

prompt: 'Database network connection fails' makes a strong extension.

distractor.0: The slides' exhibit-A reject: overly-generic problems fit every system and help no designer.

explanation: False. Extensions must be scenario-specific with step ID, handling and outcome — e.g. non-numeric data at step 5.

prompt: 'Students must finish enrolment before week 1.' Why is this not a valid NFR?
options: It governs actors, not the system — a business rule
It is actually a valid NFR

distractor.0: Its meaning is perfectly clear — clarity isn't the failure.
distractor.2: It states no reliability bound at all.
distractor.3: Check scope: who must do what?

explanation: In-scope failure: the rule constrains students, not software. Business rules look like NFRs but live outside the system boundary.

prompt: Order the five validity gates
instructions: Run every candidate NFR through these in lecture order.

items.label: Truly non-functional, not a disguised function

explanation: The Worksheet 4 Q1 verdict machine: meaning, feasibility, testability, scope, category. Fail any gate and the NFR is decoration.

prompt: Operation + bound + workload + ___ ?
instructions: Name the missing fourth part of a performance requirement.
explanation: Environment. 'Colour-enhance within 250 ms on a 10 MP image on an average PC' — drop the PC and the bound is untestable.

prompt: Match each system to its fitting metric

left.label: Forecast server over a cyclone season

pairNotes.vit: Continuous monitoring has no 'demands' — uptime fraction is the honest measure.

explanation: On-demand checks want per-attempt probability; continuous service wants uptime; long-running kit wants MTBF. Mismatches fail (2019 Q3 hint).

prompt: A reliability requirement should demand that the system never fails.

distractor.0: Perfection is untestable and unachievable — the worksheet says so explicitly. State an acceptable level for a stated failure class.

explanation: False. Reliability quantifies acceptable failure, never perfection — e.g. ≤1 min of lost vitals display per 24 h.

prompt: Match each risk to its NFR family

left.label: Vitals must reach the hospital record

explanation: Confidential → security; cross-system → interoperability; diverse abilities → accessibility. 2022 Q3.4(d) rewards exactly this risk-first reasoning.

prompt: Order the five-day plan
explanation: Marks density first (graphs, use cases), judgement last (ethics reasoning), then one closed-book rehearsal under time.

prompt: The 2022 midterm allowed calculators.

distractor.0: The cover says plainly: calculators are not allowed. Arithmetic must be hand-checkable — show working.

explanation: False — closed book, no calculators, 90 minutes, 100 marks. Method marks reward shown working even with slips.
